The sun had been a cruel, indifferent eye all day, burning the sparse alpine scrub and baking the rocks to a treacherous heat; now it sank with a swift, almost aggressive finality behind the jagged western peaks, leaving us in a sudden, profound chill. We had been making slow progress, each step an argument with the unyielding terrain, and Dr. Albright, whose intellectual fervour had thus far driven us forward, reluctantly conceded that pressing on in the deepening twilight would invite disaster. Our destination, a notoriously elusive mineral vein, lay perhaps two hours’ further climb through a labyrinth of narrow passes, a journey best undertaken with the full, merciless clarity of day. This was sensible enough, for the path ahead was riddled with sudden drops and shifting scree, and the mist, an insidious presence that had clung to the higher ridges all afternoon, now began to creep down the valleys with an unnerving purpose. Nevertheless, I felt a familiar, acid burn of frustration, not unlike the gnawing hunger in my gut, since one more night of such wretched discomfort could hardly matter after weeks spent in this desolate, god-forsaken wilderness. We had chosen a small, flat shelf beside what appeared to be the crumbling remnants of some archaic stone structure, its purpose lost to the ages, and began to make what preparations we could for the night.

The dusk itself, here in these forgotten heights, was not a gentle fading, but a swift, almost violent descent into obscurity. The air grew still, the wind, which had tormented us all day, now held its breath, and a heavy silence pressed down from the towering rock faces that enclosed us like the walls of a forgotten prison. The very stones of the ruin, lichen-crusted and pitted by millennia, seemed to absorb all sound, all light, all hope, leaving behind only an oppressive, ancient stillness. It was not peace; it was a state of profound, watchful inertia, as though the mountains themselves, along with their secret history, awaited some unspeakable unveiling. Not the faintest whisper of movement, not the rustle of a phantom rodent, could be heard. You looked on, amazed, and began to suspect yourself of being a creature of a different dimension; then the mist rolled in, soft and suffocating, and struck you blind as well.

Around midnight, a sound, unlike anything I had ever heard, tore through the thick fabric of the silence. It began as a low, resonant thrum, a vibration that seemed to emanate not from any specific point, but from the very air around us, from the cold stone beneath our bedrolls, from the marrow of our bones. It grew, slowly, inexorably, into a deeper, guttural hum, then a series of disjointed, rhythmic calls that echoed off the unseen peaks, as if the mountains themselves were clearing their ancient throats for a lament. It ceased, abruptly, leaving an unnerving void, a silence more profound than before. A few moments later, a sharp, piercing shriek, drawn out and almost musical in its dreadful intensity, sliced through the mist, making the hairs on my neck prickle under my cap. I don’t know how it struck the others; to me it seemed as though the very fog had cried out, so suddenly, and apparently from all sides at once, did this tumultuous and mournful uproar arise. It culminated in a hurried outburst of almost intolerably excessive, echoing wails, which stopped short, leaving us rigid and straining, obstinately listening to the nearly as appalling and excessive silence.

‘Good God! What in the name of,’ stammered Dr. Albright from his position near the makeshift fire, his face, even in the dim light, a ghastly white. His spectacles were askew, and his usually precise hands trembled. Milo, the youngest of us, let out a small, whimpering sound, and began to fumble for his antiquated rifle, his eyes darting frantically into the opaque whiteness, seeing nothing. He was a man of little nerve, though he imagined himself an adventurer. The two other prospectors remained frozen, their breath held, their faces etched with a fear that bordered on panic. What we could see was just our small, huddled camp, its outlines blurred as though it had been on the point of dissolving, and a milky strip of mist, perhaps ten feet thick, around us; and that was all. The rest of the world was nowhere, as far as our eyes and ears were concerned. Just nowhere. Gone, disappeared; swept off without leaving a whisper or a shadow behind.

I tightened my grip on the heavy pickaxe beside me, its cold steel a familiar comfort against the alien dread. ‘Will they attack?’ whispered Milo, his voice reedy and thin. ‘We are as good as dead in this fog,’ muttered one of the other prospectors, a burly man named Henderson, whose usual bravado had completely evaporated. Their faces twitched with the strain, their hands trembled slightly, their eyes forgot to blink, staring into the impenetrable white. It was very curious to see the contrast of expressions of the white men and of Kael, our lead guide, and his porters, who were as much strangers to these specific peaks as we, though their ancestral lands were only a few valleys away. The whites, of course greatly discomposed, had besides a curious look of being painfully shocked by such an outrageous auditory assault. The others had an alert, naturally interested expression; but their faces were essentially quiet, even those of the two young porters who grinned nervously as they nudged each other. Several exchanged short, guttural phrases, which seemed to settle the matter to their satisfaction. Kael, a tall, gaunt man with eyes like polished obsidian, and a face carved by sun and wind into an impassive mask, stood near me. He wore a patched sheepskin vest over rough spun cloth, and clutched a long, heavy staff that seemed more an extension of his own being than a mere tool.

‘They come,’ I said, my voice deliberately flat, trying to sound more confident than I felt.
‘They come,’ he echoed, his voice a low rumble, and, leaning his weight onto his staff, he gazed into the white oblivion with an unsettling composure. His eyes, devoid of fear, held only a profound, ancient knowledge.
‘Who comes, Kael?’ Dr. Albright stammered, stepping closer. ‘What *are* those sounds?’
‘Mountain spirits,’ Kael said curtly, without turning his head. ‘They guard the stone. They do not like digging.’

I would no doubt have been properly horrified by such superstitious pronouncements, had it not occurred to me that Kael and his men were not merely speaking in metaphor; that they had been hinting at the malevolent character of this particular range for days, a character we, in our scientific arrogance, had dismissed. They had been engaged for several weeks (I don’t think a single one of them had any clear idea of our ultimate objective, beyond the promise of trade goods at the journey’s end. They still belonged to the beginnings of time, had no inherited experience of the rapacious demands of progress, as we, at the end of countless ages, have); and of course, as long as there was the promise of a small payment, recorded on a scrap of paper that would be traded downriver, it didn’t enter anybody’s head to trouble how they navigated these ancient terrors. Certainly they had brought with them dried strips of game and hardened maize cakes, which couldn’t have lasted very long, anyway, even if the prospectors hadn’t, in the midst of a shocking display of panic during a recent rockfall, inadvertently sent a considerable quantity of it tumbling into a chasm. It looked like a high-handed proceeding; but it was really a case of legitimate self-preservation. One cannot breathe the acrid dust of fear, waking, sleeping, and eating, and at the same time keep one’s precarious grip on existence. Besides that, they had been given every week a handful of iron nails, each about three inches long; and the theory was they were to trade their services for provisions with that currency in remote villages. You can see how *that* worked. There were either no villages, or the people were hostile, or Dr. Albright, who like the rest of us subsisted on tins of stale biscuits and salted beef, with an occasional wild mountain goat thrown in, didn’t want to stop the expedition for some more or less recondite ethnographic study. So, unless they swallowed the nails themselves, or hammered them into their boots to climb sheer rock faces, I don’t see what good their extravagant salary could be to them. I must say it was paid with a regularity worthy of a large and honourable academic institution. For the rest, the only thing to eat, though it didn’t look edible in the least, I saw in their possession was a few lumps of some gritty, dark paste, of a dirty earthen colour, they kept wrapped in coarse leaves, and now and then swallowed a piece of, but so small that it seemed done more for the looks of the thing than for any serious purpose of sustenance. Why in the name of all the gnawing devils of hunger they didn’t turn on us, they were seven to five, and have a good tuck-in for once, amazes me now when I think of it. They were wiry, strong men, with not much capacity to weigh the consequences, with courage, with endurance, even yet, though their skin was no longer smooth and their hands were scarred by hard labour. And I saw that something restraining, one of those human secrets that baffle probability, had come into play there. I looked at them with a swift quickening of interest, not because it occurred to me I might be consumed by them before very long, though I own to you that just then I perceived, in a new light, as it were, how unwholesome the prospectors looked, and I hoped, yes, I positively hoped, that my aspect was not so, what shall I say, so unappetizing: a touch of fantastic vanity which fitted well with the dream-sensation that pervaded all my days at that time. Perhaps I had a little fever, too. One can’t live with one’s finger everlastingly on one’s pulse. I had often ‘a little fever,’ or a little touch of other things: the playful paw-strokes of the wilderness, the preliminary trifling before the more serious onslaught which came in due course. Yes; I looked at them as you would on any human.

Yes; I looked at them as you would on any human, but the light, or lack thereof, in that oppressive fog, seemed to strip away the veneer of custom and expectation, revealing something more fundamental, more ancient. It was not merely their hunger, though that gnawed at them with a persistence that beggared all human understanding of patience; it was rather the sheer, unadorned fact of their presence, their existence, in a place that seemed to actively resist any form of human imprint, that compelled my gaze. Their silence, after the initial, guttural exchange, became a part of the fog itself, dense and impenetrable, a thing that absorbed all sound and returned nothing but an amplified sense of isolation. The whites, still quivering with their peculiar blend of terror and indignation, were already, I perceived, receding from their present reality, retreating into the well-worn pathways of their own minds, where such outlandish propositions as being devoured by one’s own porters held no place in the neat schema of things. They clung to their Winchesters, to their pink pyjamas, to the very absurdities of their dress and behaviour, as if these trivialities constituted an unbreakable shield against the encroaching barbarism of their surroundings, against the truth of their predicament. They were, in their own way, as blind as the fog made us all.

But the black men, their faces etched with the stark lines of a different sort of experience, possessed a kind of awareness that was both chilling and profoundly compelling. They were not, it seemed, retreating; they were, rather, expanding, absorbing the immense, formless terror of the fog, of the unknown cries that had rent the air, into a framework of understanding entirely alien to our own. Their eyes, though bloodshot and weary from endless marches and meager rations, held a glint of something ancient, something that had seen such manifestations before, perhaps not in this precise form, but in the innumerable, subtle cruelties of a world indifferent to human suffering. The headman, still leaning on the rail with that odd, almost regal, composure, had not stirred since his blunt, unvarnished pronouncement. His gaze, fixed on the impenetrable whiteness ahead, suggested not a desire to pierce the veil of mist, but rather a profound communion with it, as if the fog itself held answers to questions we had not even dared to formulate. There was no terror in him, none of that twitching, self-conscious fear that distorted the faces of the pilgrims into grotesque caricatures of themselves. There was only a grave, watchful patience, an anticipation that was neither hopeful nor despairing, but simply was. It was then, perhaps, that the first tendrils of a truth more disturbing than any cannibalistic threat began to weave themselves into the fabric of my own consciousness: that the wilderness did not merely threaten to consume us physically, but to unravel the very threads of our supposed civility, to reveal the raw, elemental core beneath. And that these men, these ‘savages’ as we so readily termed them, were perhaps more attuned to that core, more prepared for its grim revelations, than we, with our elaborate illusions of progress and control, could ever be.

The silence that followed the wild clamour was, if anything, more unsettling than the clamour itself. It was not the mere absence of sound; it was an active, oppressive entity, pressing down upon us from all sides, suffocating the very air we breathed. It seemed to embody the immense, matted jungle, the towering multitude of trees that we had glimpsed only moments before, now swallowed once more by the unyielding fog. Each passing second of that profound quiet etched itself deeper into the memory, a testament to the primal fear that held us captive. The pilgrims, those paragons of European enterprise and ambition, shuffled their feet nervously, their whisperings hushed and sporadic, like the rustle of dry leaves in a windless grove. They cast anxious glances at each other, at the impenetrable wall of white, and then, with an almost comical uniformity, at their rifles, as if the mere possession of these instruments of death could dispel the formless dread that clung to them. One, the little fat man with the sandy hair, who had stammered earlier, now found a fresh subject for his terror in the black fellows themselves. His eyes, darting with suspicion, would settle for a moment on their calm, impassive faces, then flit away as if afraid to meet their gaze. He saw, I surmised, not men who might defend him, but an additional, equally inscrutable threat, perhaps even more immediate in its proximity than the unseen terror in the mist.

The fog itself, warm and clammy as it was, became a character in this silent drama, an accomplice to the unseen forces that had unleashed the shriek and the ensuing quiet. It did not merely obscure; it transformed. Our steamer, a robust vessel of iron and steam, became a phantom ship, its outlines blurred, its solidity questioned by the pervasive shroud. The small strip of water around us, perhaps two feet broad, shimmered with an eerie, phosphorescent quality, reflecting nothing but the milky oblivion above. The rest of the world, indeed, was nowhere. This absolute obliteration of all landmarks, of all familiar reference points, served to amplify the sense of precariousness, of being suspended not merely in space, but in a strange, unmoored dimension of time. One lost the sense of hours, of direction, of purpose, all subsumed by the insistent, featureless presence of the white. It was as if the world had shrunk to this single, pulsating point of our existence, a fragile bubble of consciousness adrift in an ocean of unreasoning chaos.

The manager, a man whose every action was usually dictated by a meticulous calculation of profit and loss, now moved with an unusual, almost hesitant gait. His customary air of cool authority seemed to have been momentarily displaced by a vague uneasiness, a shadow of uncertainty that flitted across his usually impassive features. He too, I observed, cast furtive glances at the impenetrable wall of white, though he quickly composed himself, adjusting his collar with a familiar gesture of reasserted control. He mumbled something about the chain, about ensuring the anchor held fast, though his voice lacked its usual crisp command, dissipating into the heavy air like a wisp of smoke. He was a man of systems, of ledgers and inventories, and this situation, this formless, unquantifiable menace, was clearly outside the scope of his meticulously constructed world. It was a testament, I thought, to the insidious power of the wilderness, that it could momentarily dislodge even the most deeply entrenched convictions of European practicality. He was, for all his rank and position, as much a prisoner of the fog as any of us, though he would have died, I believe, rather than admit to such an unmanly capitulation to the unknown.

My own thoughts, meanwhile, drifted from the immediate peril, though it never entirely receded, to a more expansive contemplation of the nature of our journey itself. What were we, really, doing here? What colossal, insatiable hunger drove us, Europeans, into these remote, inhospitable corners of the earth, dragging with us our absurd notions of progress and our fragile sense of superiority? We were, I suddenly perceived, like children playing with fire in a vast, dry forest, utterly oblivious to the immensity of the forces we were so blithely disturbing. The clamour, that ‘cry of infinite desolation,’ as I had instinctively termed it, resonated not merely as a sound in the air, but as an echo within the deeper chambers of my own being, a recognition of something ancient and terrifyingly true about this land, about perhaps all lands, that lay buried beneath the thin crust of our modern existence. It was not the cry of a beast, not purely, nor even the cry of a human, in the way we understood humanity; it was, rather, the voice of the wilderness itself, a primal scream of resistance against our intrusive presence, a warning, perhaps, of the profound, unfathomable darkness that awaited those who dared to penetrate its sacred, forgotten sanctuaries. And in that moment, in the oppressive stillness of the fog, I felt a peculiar, almost exhilarating sense of recognition, as if I had, for the first time, truly heard the voice of this colossal, brooding entity that surrounded us, patiently waiting.

The headman, having delivered his chilling pronouncement about the destination of any caught perpetrators of the noise, a pronouncement delivered with such a matter-of-fact solemnity that it momentarily stunned even me, now remained perfectly still. His men, too, were quiet, their movements minimal, almost ritualistic, as they secured the chain once more. There was no fuss, no agitation, merely an acceptance of the moment, whatever it might bring. It was a disquieting contrast to the spasmodic anxieties of the whites, who, even in their moments of relative calm, seemed unable to shed the nervous energy that was, I now suspected, not merely a response to the immediate threat, but an intrinsic characteristic of their ‘civilized’ existence. They were perpetually on edge, perpetually striving, perpetually fearful of what lay beyond the familiar boundaries of their neatly ordered world. The black fellows, on the other hand, appeared to inhabit a different order of reality, one in which the distinction between the familiar and the unknown was less sharply drawn, where the whispers of the jungle and the cries of unseen creatures were not necessarily portents of doom, but simply elements of a larger, more encompassing design. They possessed, I began to surmise, a kind of primal wisdom, a deep, intuitive understanding of their surroundings that transcended our own intellectual categories, our scientific classifications, our arrogant assumptions of mastery. They were children of the earth, intimately connected to its rhythms, its furies, its indifferent majesties, in a way that we, with our brass wire and our tins of stale biscuits, could never hope to be. They had no need for theories of survival; they simply survived, drawing upon an ancestral reservoir of resilience and cunning that predated all our recorded histories, all our finely wrought philosophies.

The waiting in the fog was not a passive state; it was an active, corrosive process, slowly eating away at the edges of one’s sanity. The humid air, thick and cloying, seemed to stifle not only breath but thought itself, reducing the mind to a state of dull, insistent apprehension. Every faint rustle from the unseen banks, every indistinct gurgle of the current, was magnified a hundredfold by the heightened senses, transformed into a potential harbinger of renewed terror. The sound of our own breathing, the faint creak of the steamer’s hull, became unnaturally loud, alien, as if emanating from some distant, unfamiliar mechanism. The sun, I knew, must be climbing, but its light, so eagerly anticipated, remained a tantalizing, ethereal glow behind the impenetrable curtain of white. It was a mockery of dawn, a false promise of illumination that only served to deepen the pervasive sense of unreality. The pilgrims, those paragons of colonial endeavor, grew increasingly agitated, their earlier bravado having dissolved into a pitiable display of nervous tics and whispered lamentations. They spoke of rescue, of the distant, comforting world of their homes, of wives and children, as if these domestic phantoms could somehow conjure a pathway through the formless terror that encompassed us. Their words, however, sounded hollow, insubstantial, mere wisps of sound that dissolved without an echo in the dense, silent air. They clung to their memories, to their expectations, to the fragile edifice of their ‘normalcy’ with a desperation that was both pathetic and, in its own way, profoundly human.

And I, watching this spectacle of fear and a strange, almost barbaric calm, felt a curious detachment, an observer removed, as it were, from the immediate currents of emotion that surged through the vessel. The fever, that persistent, low-grade companion of my journey, seemed to sharpen my perceptions even as it dulled my physical senses, lending a dream-like quality to the entire experience. It was as if I were peering through a veil, beholding not merely the current situation, but a deeper, more profound truth about existence itself. This wilderness, this immense, brooding presence, was not merely a physical landscape; it was a state of being, a primordial force that stripped away all the layers of acquired habit and societal convention, revealing the stark, elemental core of human nature. It was a mirror, reflecting back not what we wished to see, but what we truly were, in our most naked, most vulnerable, most unadorned state. The absurdity of our mission, the futility of our struggles against such an overwhelming, indifferent power, became blindingly clear in that all-encompassing white void. We were but transient specks, momentary disturbances in an ancient, timeless order, destined to be reabsorbed, forgotten, leaving no trace upon its vast, immutable expanse. The brass wire, the tins of food, the Winchesters, the very steamer beneath our feet, all seemed utterly meaningless, pathetic trinkets wielded by ignorant children in the face of an omnipotent, unforgiving deity. The silence, which had seemed so unnerving, now began to acquire a different quality, a kind of profound, encompassing peace, as if the wilderness, having spoken its terrible truth, now simply rested, content in its ultimate, unquestionable dominion.

It was at this point, when the oppressive stillness had reached its zenith, when the silence had begun to penetrate not merely the ear but the very soul, that a subtle change began to manifest itself in the pervasive white shroud. Not a sudden lifting, not a dramatic dissipation, but a gradual, almost imperceptible thinning, as if the immense, solid curtain were slowly, reluctantly, becoming translucent. The light, which had been a uniform, featureless glow, now gained a hint of texture, a suggestion of depth, though no specific forms were yet discernible. They spoke of rites, of ceremonies, of a collective consciousness that predated any notion of individual existence, of a profound and terrible unity with the earth.

Their initial bravado, never much to begin with, had long since evaporated, leaving behind a brittle shell of nervous tics and forced jocularity. They had become creatures of impulse and raw, unvarnished fear. The Winchesters, once symbols of their supposed mastery over this savage land, were now clutched like sacred talismans, aimed vaguely at the impenetrable wall of vegetation that hemmed us in. Their eyes, bloodshot and dilated, perpetually scanned the banks, seeking, I suppose, some tangible enemy, something that could be met with a bullet and a shout, something comprehensible within their narrow, self-serving universe. Another, a gaunt, dark-haired fellow with perpetually pursed lips, spent his days sharpening a long hunting knife, his movements becoming increasingly obsessive and ritualistic, as if the mere act of honing steel could somehow carve a path through the psychological jungle that surrounded us.

They seemed to possess an innate understanding of the river’s moods, of the jungle’s secrets. The drums, which drove the whites to distraction, seemed to stir in them a different, perhaps older, kind of recognition. Their headman, the powerful young man with the oiled ringlets and the fierce nostrils, stood often at the bow, his gaze fixed on the shifting patterns of the current, his bearing one of profound, unshakeable dignity. He, at least, acknowledged the raw, elemental forces of existence, the hunger that gnawed at the core of all living things, without the elaborate pretense of “civilized” consumption.

My own mind, though not yet entirely surrendered to the feverish dream of the river, felt the insidious tug of unreality. The days blurred into one another, marked only by the shifting intensity of the heat and the ceaseless, hypnotic rhythm of the drums. My thoughts drifted, unmoored from the familiar anchors of purpose and progress. I found myself contemplating the very nature of truth, of illusion, of the thin, porous membrane that separated one from the other in this land where shadows seemed more substantial than substance. Kurtz, that enigmatic figure, grew in my imagination with an almost supernatural intensity. He was no longer merely a man, a Company agent; he was a projected image, a living myth, a vessel for all the unspoken horrors and hidden potentials of this vast, untamed continent. He was the end-point of this journey, the ultimate revelation, a mirror held up to the darkest corners of the human soul.

We passed an abandoned station, its bamboo structures sagging, overgrown with vines, its clearing reclaimed by the relentless encroachment of the jungle. It was a silent testament to futile effort, to the ephemeral nature of man’s dominion in the face of such overwhelming power. A sense of desolation, palpable and profound, hung in the air, a spiritual stench of hopes withered and ambitions devoured. There were no signs of violence, no shattered remnants of conflict, only the slow, inexorable triumph of green oblivion. It was as if the earth itself had simply inhaled, drawing back into its immense lungs all that man had dared to deposit upon its surface. The pilgrims pointed with trembling fingers, their whispers like dry leaves skittering across the deck, seeing in the ruins their own impending doom, their own fragile insignificance. But I saw something else, a premonition of Kurtz’s own fate, perhaps, or a glimpse into the terrible freedom of a man who had shed the last vestiges of that fleeting dominion.

The current grew swifter, the river narrower, as if compressing itself for a final, intense surge into the heart of the land. The banks rose higher, a dizzying wall of ancient trees that seemed to scrape the very sky, their canopy so dense that the sun was reduced to a flickering, distant memory, casting only dappled, shifting patterns of light and shadow upon the water. The air grew stiller, heavier, pregnant with an unspoken anticipation. The jungle here was different; it possessed a brooding intensity, an ancient, watchful presence that felt less like passive vegetation and more like a conscious, breathing entity. The sounds, too, were subtly altered. The buzzing of insects, the chirping of birds, which had previously formed a constant, if unnoticed, accompaniment, now seemed muted, suppressed, as if even the smallest creatures held their breath.

And the drums. They were no longer merely rhythmic; they had become a symphony of disquiet, a complex tapestry of interlocking beats, some deep and resonant, others sharp and percussive, all of them converging into a single, overwhelming chorus that vibrated through the very core of one’s being. There was a message in them, an undeniable communication, though its language was one of pure sensation, a primal lexicon understood by the nerves and the blood, rather than by the intellect. It was the sound of a world utterly alien, utterly self-contained, a world complete unto itself, needing nothing from the transient intrusions of European ambition.

A hush, profound and absolute, had fallen over the jungle, a silence so complete that it seemed to absorb all other sound, even the distant, persistent thrum of the drums. It was a silence that was not empty, but full, pregnant with meaning, a silence that felt like a deliberate act, a conscious withholding of breath. The pilgrims huddled together, their faces pale and drawn in the dying light, their eyes wide with an unspoken terror. They sensed it too, the change in the very fabric of the air, the profound gravity of the moment.

Then, from the darkness of the trees, a single, sharp sound cut through the stillness. It was not a drum, nor a human cry, but something else entirely, a metallic clang, followed by a series of hurried, guttural shouts. It was brief, instantly subsumed by the resumed, watchful silence. My heart gave a curious, anticipatory lurch, a mixture of dread and an almost perverse excitement. The reckoning was near.

He wiped a hand across his sweating brow, leaving a streak of grime. “They are close,” he whispered, his voice thin and reedy in the immense silence. “Very close now.” His eyes, normally shifty and calculating, held a flicker of genuine fear, a rare sight that lent a grim authenticity to his words. He was, after all, a creature of the Company, a purveyor of its meager, tawdry realities, and even he felt the pressure of this alien world.

"For the meat," he said, finally, his voice still low, almost a murmur, yet imbued with an unmistakable gravitas, "The meat of the river. The meat of the land. The meat of the white men."

My blood, I confess, ran cold, not from fear, not from the immediate threat of physical violence, but from the profound, unsettling simplicity of his statement, from the sheer, unblinking clarity of his understanding. It was not a threat, not an act of aggression, but a statement of elemental truth, a brutal, undeniable logic that flowed as inexorably as the river itself. The wilderness, in its infinite, indifferent wisdom, provided. And what it provided, it expected to be consumed, whether it was the flesh of beasts, the fruits of the soil, or, in moments of desperation, the very flesh of men. It was a logic that bypassed all the elaborate constructions of civilised morality, all the intricate sophistries of conquest and exploitation. It was a logic that reduced existence to its most basic, most terrifying denominator: hunger and its satisfaction, life and its inevitable consumption.

The white men, meanwhile, had begun to stir, a nervous, agitated fidgeting that contrasted sharply with the unmoving stillness of the figures on the bank. They had perhaps not heard the headman's quiet words, or, if they had, they had dismissed them as the incoherent mutterings of a "savage," a mere further confirmation of their preconceived notions of barbarism. They clung instead to the outward symbols of their supposed superiority, their Winchesters, their uniforms, their ingrained habits of command, even in the face of a situation that rendered all such symbols utterly meaningless. They were like children playing at soldiers, brandishing toy weapons against an enemy that existed not in the realm of their childish games, but in the dark, unfathomable depths of a primordial world.

I watched them, these pilgrims, with a renewed sense of their profound, almost tragic, inadequacy. They were adrift, hopelessly lost, not merely in the geographical immensity of the jungle, but in the moral and intellectual wilderness that it represented. Their fear, so palpable, so utterly incapacitating, was not merely a fear of death, but a fear of dissolution, a terror of being stripped bare, of being reduced to the same elemental, hungry state as the "savages" they so despised, so condescendingly dismissed. They feared the truth that the headman had so succinctly articulated, the truth that their own elaborate structures of civilisation were but a fragile, temporary veneer over a deeper, more brutal reality, a reality that the wilderness, in its relentless, indifferent manner, was now forcing them to confront.

A ripple of movement, slight and almost imperceptible, ran through the figures on the bank. It was not a hostile movement, not an advance, but rather a slow, deliberate shifting, a subtle rearrangement of their positions, as if they were settling in, preparing for a long, patient vigil. Their eyes, I imagined, though still unseen, remained fixed on our steamer, on this incongruous intrusion of metal and smoke into their timeless domain. They were waiting, I knew, not with impatience, not with any overt threat, but with the profound, almost geological patience of the wilderness itself, a patience that could outlast empires, outwait generations, a patience that knew, with an ancient, undeniable certainty, that all things, eventually, came to them.

The sun, now climbing higher in the immense, humid sky, beat down with a relentless intensity, turning the air into a shimmering, incandescent haze. The sounds of the jungle, previously subdued, now began to swell, a gradual, insidious chorus of unseen insects, distant bird calls, and the almost imperceptible rustlings of unseen creatures within the dense foliage. It was a sound that was not loud, not overt, but rather a pervasive, insistent hum, a living, breathing symphony of the wild, a constant, murmuring reminder of the immeasurable, indifferent vitality that surrounded us. It was a sound that, like the profound silence that had preceded it, seemed to penetrate the very marrow of one's bones, speaking of depths and mysteries that defied all human comprehension, all civilised categories.

I turned from the rail, my gaze sweeping over the deck, over the agitated, fear-stricken faces of the white men, over the stoic, enigmatic countenances of the black crew, over the pathetic array of their futile weapons and their meaningless provisions. We were, I knew, suspended in a moment of profound, almost unbearable tension, a moment poised precariously between the known and the utterly unfathomable. The immediate danger, the threat of an outright attack, seemed, paradoxically, to recede, replaced by a deeper, more insidious dread, a sense of being utterly exposed, utterly vulnerable, to the vast, indifferent, and ultimately incomprehensible forces of the wilderness. It was a dread that seeped into the very soul, a chilling premonition of the slow, inexorable dissolution of all that we held dear, all that we considered "civilised," all that we believed to be the unshakeable foundations of our existence. And at the heart of that dissolution, at the very nexus of that terrifying truth, lay the unsettling, resonant whisper of a name: Kurtz, the man who had ventured furthest into this heart of darkness, the man who had, perhaps, dared to embrace the very unspeakable hungers that now seemed to rise, shimmering and vast, from the emerald depths of the immense, matted jungle. The chain, which I had ordered hauled in, then paid out again, lay slack and heavy on the deck, a symbol of our arrested progress, our enforced pause at the very threshold of the unknown, of the terrifying, ultimate revelation that awaited us further up the river, in the very heart of that profound, unsettling stillness.
